cues.text: A Childhood Marked by Loss
Born Karol Józef Wojtyła in 1920 in Wadowice, Poland, the future pope endured repeated family tragedy in youth.
His mother died when he was eight, and his older brother, a doctor, died of scarlet fever when he was twelve.

Raised largely by his devout father, whose austere, prayerful example he later called 'my first seminary,' Karol was a gifted student and athlete who loved theater and poetry, enrolling at Kraków's Jagiellonian University in 1938.
Underground Seminary Under Nazi Occupation

When Nazi Germany invaded Poland in 1939, Karol worked in a stone quarry and chemical factory to avoid deportation, while secretly participating in underground theater as a form of cultural resistance.
In 1942, discerning a vocation to the priesthood, he began clandestine seminary studies organized in secret by the Archbishop of Kraków, unable to attend an official seminary under German occupation.
Rising Through a Communist State
Ordained in 1946, Wojtyła earned doctorates in theology and philosophy and taught ethics at Kraków's Catholic University.
He rose steadily through the Church hierarchy under an increasingly repressive Communist government, becoming Archbishop of Kraków in 1964 and a cardinal in 1967.
Throughout, he built a reputation as an effective, quietly determined defender of religious freedom against state pressure.
Election as Pope
Following the sudden deaths of Pope Paul VI and then Pope John Paul I in 1978, after only thirty-three days, the College of Cardinals elected the fifty-eight-year-old Wojtyła.
He was the first non-Italian pope in over four centuries and the only Polish pope in history, and took the name John Paul II .
'Be Not Afraid' and the Fall of Communism

John Paul II's 1979 pilgrimage to his native Poland, drawing enormous crowds despite Communist government disapproval, is widely credited by historians with galvanizing the Solidarity movement that ultimately helped bring down Communist rule across Eastern Europe by 1989.
He survived an assassination attempt in St. Peter's Square in 1981, later personally forgiving and visiting his would-be assassin in prison.
He went on to become history's most-traveled pope, visiting some 129 countries over a twenty-six-year pontificate — the second-longest in Church history.
Legacy
John Paul II died at the Vatican on April 2, 2005, after a long, publicly visible struggle with Parkinson's disease.
He canonized more saints during his pontificate than all his predecessors combined and left behind substantial encyclicals.
These included influential teaching on human dignity and the 'theology of the body.'
Pope Francis canonized him in 2014.
For many, he remains simply 'John Paul the Great' — a pope whose personal courage helped reshape the map of twentieth-century Europe.
